body.p: EntriesHeadings Indexes comprise two main parts: the index headnote and the entries themselves.

section.title: Headnotes
section.p: Headnotes Headnotes are used to alert readers to any unusual or nonstandard practices in the index. Headnotes may cover such items as use of special typography (“Page numbers in italics refer to illustrations”), abbreviations, or locator formatting. Headnotes may also indicate special issues of coverage (“Names of fictional characters have not been indexed”).

section.title: Index Entries
section.p: Entriescomponents of Index entries consist of three parts: headings, subheadings, and locators.

Headings Entriesheadings Headings are the terms that lead users to information. Headings typically consist of nouns or noun phrases; adjectives or adverbs rarely make useful headings. Headings should also express complete concepts and should provide access both to high-level topics as well as to more specific details.

Subheadings Entriessubheadings Subheadings (also called subentries) provide a second level of access to information. There is no strict rule about when subheadings should be used, but a general guideline is that any main heading with five or more undifferentiated locators should probably have subheadings created for it.

Locators Entrieslocators Complex locators Locators tell the reader where to find the specific information indicated by the heading and/or subheading. Locators are most often page numbers but can include section numbers, paragraph numbers, or other pointers to a specific location in the text.

section.title: Cross-References
section.p: Cross-referencestypes of Cross-referencessee references Cross-referencessee also references Cross-references are signposts in the index. They direct users from one place in the index to another. There are two types: See references and See also references.
A See reference directs the reader from a term that is not used in the index to the term that is used. For example: “Dogs. See Canines.”
A See also reference directs the reader from one term to a related term where additional information can be found. For example: “Dogs. See also Wolves.”

Blind cross-references Cross-referencesblind Circular cross-references Cross-referencescircular Generic cross-references Cross-referencesgeneric Blind cross-references are those that lead nowhere—references to headings that do not exist in the index. Circular cross-references create an endless loop. Generic cross-references suggest types of entries to look for rather than pointing to a specific heading.

Double-posting Double-postingCross-references The alternative to a cross-reference is double-posting, where the same locators are placed under two or more headings. Double-posting is generally preferred when the number of locators is small.
